sections.h2: Where is Ouachita Parish and what towns does it include?
sections.html:
Ouachita Parish sits in northern Louisiana, and its parish seat is Monroe, which is also its largest municipality. West Monroe lies across the Ouachita River from Monroe, and the two cities are the parish's only incorporated cities. The towns are Richwood and Sterlington.

Wikipedia gives the parish a total area of 632 square miles, with 610 of them land. The 2020 census counted 160,368 people, and the 2025 estimate is 158,542. Interstate 20, U.S. 80 and U.S. 165 cross the parish.

Neighbors are Union Parish to the north, Morehouse to the northeast, Richland to the east, Caldwell to the south, Jackson to the southwest and Lincoln to the west. Unincorporated communities that appear on property records include Bawcomville, Brownsville, Calhoun, Claiborne, Lakeshore and Swartz.

sections.h2: What shaped the Ouachita Parish housing stock?
sections.html:
Housing in the parish reflects several waves of growth. Wikipedia reports that the Monroe natural gas field was discovered in 1916 and covered more than 500 square miles. For a time Monroe was known as the natural gas capital of the world.

The population of the parish rose by more than 79 percent between 1920 and 1930, to roughly 54,000 people, as workers arrived. The census figures in the same article show the parish passing 100,000 residents in 1960 and reaching 160,368 in 2020.

A railroad bridge over the river opened in 1883, and Sterlington and Richwood were incorporated in 1961 and 1974. A seller with a house from any of these building waves should expect the age of the roof, wiring and plumbing to shape what a buyer asks for.

sections.h2: Who works in Ouachita Parish and what does it mean for sellers?
sections.html:
Wikipedia, citing the North Louisiana Economic Partnership, lists a mix of technology, health care, government, finance and manufacturing employers at the top of the parish.

The University of Louisiana at Monroe is also in Monroe. Public schools outside Monroe are run by the Ouachita Parish School Board, and the Monroe City School System serves areas within Monroe. Which district a house falls in depends on its address, so check before you describe schools to a buyer.

sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Ouachita Parish?
sections.html:
The Ouachita Parish Assessor values property, and the Ouachita Parish Sheriff collects the tax. The Louisiana Constitution and Legislature set the framework, and the Louisiana Tax Commission writes the assessment rules. Local bodies such as the police jury and school board set the levies that appear on a bill.

Ouachita Parish AssessorLists and values all taxable property, tracks homestead exemptionsAssessor Stephanie Smith; records searchable online

The Assessor's website at opassessor.com carries a property search, an interactive map, millage rates by ward and a tax calculator. The Sheriff's office posts tax information at opso.net.

sections.h2: How is a Ouachita Parish assessment worked out?
sections.html:
The Assessor takes fair market value and multiplies it by a statutory percentage. According to the Assessor's FAQ, land is assessed at 10 percent of fair market value and residential improvements at 10 percent. Commercial property, including personal property, is at 15 percent, though commercial land is at 10 percent.

The office gives a worked example. A $100,000 home is assessed at $10,000. After the $7,500 maximum homestead exemption, the taxable value is $2,500, and at 120 mills the parish taxes are $300. The office adds that the homestead exemption does not reduce city taxes, so a house inside Monroe or West Monroe can see a higher total than a house outside them.

Louisiana requires reassessment at least every four years, and a property can be reassessed at any time after a sale or a change. The Assessor also asks new buyers to complete a Sales Questionnaire, which helps check fair market value.

sections.h2: When are Ouachita Parish property taxes due?
sections.html:
Under Louisiana's general rule, bills go out in December and taxes are due December 31, with interest of 1 percent per month on late balances. The House Fiscal Division's property tax summary states those terms for parishes statewide.

The Sheriff's office is the collector, and the Tax Office takes payments by mail, in person or online.

The Assessor's FAQ warns that a missing notice does not excuse payment. If you did not receive a bill, you can ask the tax collector what is owed.

  • Bills are mailed once a year, in December.
  • Late balances accrue interest at 1 percent a month.
  • Unpaid property can go to a tax sale, and a debtor has three years to redeem immovable property sold that way.
  • Foreclosure and seizure sales run through the Sheriff's Civil Division, with auctions on Wednesday mornings at 10 a.m. through an online platform.

sections.h2: How do you challenge a Ouachita Parish assessment?
sections.html:
Talk to the Assessor first, then appeal to the Ouachita Parish Board of Review if the disagreement stays. After that, an appeal can go to the Louisiana Tax Commission, and finally to the courts.

The Assessor's office asks owners to bring evidence that its valuation is wrong. Recent sale prices, an appraisal and photographs of damage are the kinds of material that other Louisiana boards accept. Louisiana law lets the public inspect the tax roll in a window between August 15 and September 15 outside Orleans Parish.

Missing the appeal window usually means waiting for the next tax year.

sections.h2: What exemptions can lower a Ouachita Parish tax bill?
sections.html:
The main reductions are the homestead exemption and the special assessment freeze for older owners. The homestead exemption is $7,500 of assessed value, which equals $75,000 of market value, for an owner-occupied home. It can cover up to 160 acres that include an owner-occupied residence.

The Assessor's website links to an application postcard and a page about the 65 and older Special Assessment Value Freeze. State guidance says the freeze can also apply to owners with a service-connected disability of at least 50 percent, subject to an income limit. The Assessor also publishes a veterans brochure. A buyer needs to apply on his or her own, since both benefits are tied to the person living in the home.

sections.h2: What should you know about selling a Ouachita Parish house with tax due?
sections.html:
Unpaid taxes are a lien on the property and must be cleared for a clean title to pass. Under La. R.S. 47:1993, once the assessment roll is delivered to the recorder of mortgages, it acts as a lien and privilege on each assessed property, and it generally ranks ahead of other encumbrances.

In practice the closing attorney or title company asks the Sheriff's Tax Office for a payoff and pays it from the proceeds. Deeds are recorded with the Ouachita Parish Clerk of Court, whose office is on South Grand Street in Monroe. If the house also carries a mortgage, back taxes and repairs, the title work can take longer, so start the payoff request early.

Check the Assessor's property search for your parcel's current owner and homestead status before you list. Errors found there are easier to fix before a buyer's attorney finds them.

faqs.q: When are Ouachita Parish property taxes due?
faqs.a: The general Louisiana rule is December 31, and late balances accrue 1 percent interest per month. Confirm the exact year's deadline with the Ouachita Parish Sheriff's Tax Office at (318) 324-2536.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Ouachita Parish?
faqs.a: The Ouachita Parish Sheriff, acting as ex-officio tax collector. Payments can be made by mail, in person or online through the Sheriff's website.

faqs.q: What is the Ouachita Parish homestead exemption?
faqs.a: It is $7,500 of assessed value, equal to $75,000 of fair market value, on an owner-occupied home. The Assessor's FAQ says it does not apply to city taxes.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Ouachita Parish assessment?
faqs.a: Meet with the Assessor, then appeal to the Ouachita Parish Board of Review, then to the Louisiana Tax Commission.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay?
faqs.a: Interest accrues at 1 percent a month, and the property can be sold at a tax sale. A debtor has three years to redeem immovable property sold that way.

faqs.q: Do I owe property tax at closing in Ouachita Parish?
faqs.a: Unpaid taxes are a lien and have to be cleared for clear title, so the balance is normally paid from the sale proceeds. Your closing attorney or title company will request the figure from the Tax Office.
